BILL NUMBER:  S3258

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the public health law, in relation to the sale,
delivery, dispensing and/or distribution of controlled substances


 PURPOSE :

This bill will: (1) enhance efforts to curtail the diversion, abuse
and illegal sale of prescription controlled substances by authorizing
the Department of Health (DOH) to notify a pharmacy that a patient has
obtained a prescription for controlled substances from another
pharmacy; (2) curtail prescription drug diversion by authorizing the
sharing of official prescription information with authorized
controlled substance regulatory agencies in other states; (3) make
conforming technical amendments to the existing statutory authority
for electronic prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances;
(4) curtail the diversion, abuse and illegal sale of human growth
hormone, anabolic steroids, and pregabalin by designating them as
controlled substances; and (5) update reporting requirements for
methadone treatment programs.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill amends Public Health Law (PHL) §§ 3302(9) and
(10) to expand the definition of "dispense" and "distribute" to
include Internet transactions.

Section 2 of the bill adds new PHL § 3302(34), (35), (36), (37), (38)
and (39) to define terms pertaining to Internet transactions.

Section 3 of the bill adds new PHL § 3335 to provide that online
dispensers must comply with PHL Article 33 and must submit information
about the dispensing of controlled substances to DOH by electronic
means.

Section 4 amends PHL § 3371(1) to authorize DOH to notify a pharmacy
when a person who presents a prescription for a controlled substance
at the pharmacy may have also obtained controlled substances at other
pharmacies.

Section 5 of the bill adds new PHL § 3371-a to authorize DOH to share
information about prescription controlled substances with authorized
controlled substance regulatory agencies in other states under defined
circumstances and for specified purposes.

Section 6 of the bill amends PHL §§ 3331(6) to maintain the existing
requirement that information regarding the dispensing of Controlled
substances be filed electronically with DOH, subject to DOH
regulations, but eliminate the statutory requirement that the
information he filed within a particular time period.

Section 7 of the bill amends PHL § 3332 to authorize health care
practitioners to prescribe controlled substances by electronic means
and describe the information that must be included in such electronic
prescription such as the name and address of both the practitioner and
the patient and the date of prescription.

Section 8 of the bill amends PHL § 3333 to authorize pharmacies to
dispense controlled substances prescribed electronically. The section
maintains the requirement that the pharmacy electronically file
prescription information with DOH regarding the dispensing of
controlled substances but eliminates the requirement that the
information be filed within a particular time period.

Section 9 of the bill amends PHL § 3370 to require that electronic
prescription records be maintained as required by regulations of the
Commissioner of Health.

Sections 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the bill make technical conforming
amendments to PHL §§ .3334,33.37 and both versions of 3381 (one
version expires September 1, 2011 and the other takes effect on that
date) to reflect the new statutory scheme for the electronic
prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances.

Sections 14 through 20 of the bill amend PHL § 3306 by updating the
controlled substance schedules.

Section 21 of the bill amends PHL § 3352 to delete the requirement
that a Methadone Maintenance Treatment Program (MMTP) file a monthly
report with DOH summarizing all methadone activity from the previous
month, while retaining the requirement that instances of theft, loss
or possible diversion of controlled substances be immediately
reported. The section also removes a reference in PHL § 3352 to
Article 23 of the Mental Hygiene Law (MHL), which was repealed a
number of years ago.

Section 22 of the bill provides that the bill will take effect
immediately, except that §§ 1 through 3 and 21 will take effect 180
days after the bill's enactment and §§ 14 through 20 will take effect
90 days after the bill's enactment.

 EXISTING LAW :

PHL § 3302 sets forth definitions applicable to PHL Article 33.

PHL § 3306 establishes five schedules listing controlled substances.
Schedule I controlled substances may not be prescribed, dispensed,
possessed, distributed or administered except for research purposes
with the approval of DOH. Substances listed on Schedules II, III, IV,
and V may be prescribed only by authorized practitioners.

PHL § 3308 authorizes DOH to promulgate regulations regarding the
prescribing, dispensing. use and transmission of electronic
prescriptions.

PHL § 3331(6) requires practitioners that dispense controlled
substances to file information related to such dispensing with DOH by
electronic means.

PHL § 3332 provides that prescriptions for controlled substances can
only be made in writing on an official New York State prescription
form.

PHL § 3333(4) requires pharmacies to file information related to the
dispensing of controlled substances with DOH by electronic means.

PHL §§ 3334 and 3337 authorize oral prescriptions for controlled
substances in emergency situations, so long as a written prescription
is delivered to the dispensing pharmacy within 72 hours.

PHL § 3338 authorizes the prescribing and dispensing of controlled
substances pursuant to electronic prescriptions, in accordance with
regulations of the Commissioner.

PHL § 3352 requires MMTPs to maintain records showing the receipt,
administration, dispensing, or destruction of all controlled
substances to submit monthly reports of methadone activity to DOH,
including information about thefts or losses.


PHL § 3371 authorizes DOH to notify a practitioner when a person under
his or her treatment with controlled substances also may be under
treatment with controlled substances by another practitioner.

PHL § 3370 requires the maintenance of records concerning prescription
controlled substances.

PHL § 3381 concerns the sale and possession of hypodermic syringes and
hypodermic needles. Certain sections of the version of § 3381 that is
currently in effect will be replaced by a second version on September
1, 2011, pursuant to Chapter 56 of the Laws of 2000.

MHL §§ 32.05 and 32.09 require operating certificates for MMTPs.

Title 10, § 80.73(t) of the New York Codes, Rules and Regulations
(NYCRR) requires that electronic prescriptions for controlled
substances be transmitted in a transmission format acceptable to DOH.

The regulations of the State Education Department at 8 NYCRR §
63.6(a)(7) permit electronic prescriptions for non-controlled
substances, as long as the transmission of a prescription from a
prescriber to a pharmacy is selected through electronic encryption.

Title 42, Part 160 of the Code of Federal Regulations requires health
care providers that transmit protected health information
electronically to encrypt such transmissions.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

A.11690, S.8185-A, which contained most of the components indicated in
this bill, passed the Senate but not the Assembly in 2008.
A.10666-A/S.8186-A,which contained the provision on MMTPs, passed the
Assembly but not the Senate in 2008.

 STATEMENT IN SUPPORT :

A. Pharmacy Notification Program

Under its Official Prescription Program, DOH notifies practitioners
when a patient obtains controlled substances from multiple
practitioners within 30 days, a situation which may indicate possible
drug abuse or the criminal diversion of drugs. To date, DOH has
notified nearly 9,000 practitioners regarding more than 1,600
patients. Many states, including Ohio, California, Kentucky, and
Nevada have similar programs, and Nevada's program has reduced such
drug seeking activity by 65 percent. The proposed amendment to PHL
§3371, authorizing DOH to notify pharmacies of patients utilizing
multiple pharmacies, will similarly enhance efforts to curtail the
diversion and abuse of controlled substances.

B. Sharing of Information with Authorized Out-of-State Entities

This bill will allow DOH to provide official prescription information
to authorized controlled substance regulatory agencies in other
states. Providing this information will curtail prescription dnJg
diversion by individuals engaging in drug seeking activity in multiple
states.  The legislation will also make New York eligible for millions
of dollars in federal funding available under a federal law entitled
the National All Schedules Prescription Electronic Reporting (NASPER).
The purpose of NASPER is to curtail drug diversion through the
establishment and enhancement of prescription monitoring programs and
through the sharing of prescription monitoring program data between
states. This bill will allow DOH to share official prescription data
with authorized agencies from other states which agree to comply with
DOH standards, including adherence to strict security, authentication
of information, and strict confidentiality of data.
C. Electronic Prescriptions for Controlled Substances

An estimated 15 to 20 percent of all paper prescriptions are
fraudulent. Electronic prescribing is a secure method of transmitting
prescriptions from practitioners to pharmacists and curtails
prescription fraud because an electronic prescription cannot be
physically altered, forged, or stolen by individuals attempting to
divert controlled substances for addiction and illegal sale.  Equally
important, electronic prescribing enhances patient care by minimizing
medication errors due to misinterpretations of handwriting on written
prescriptions. It is estimated that 20 percent of the approximately
7,000 annual deaths caused by medication errors are attributed to
misinterpretations of written prescriptions. In addition to the
unnecessary loss of life, medication errors are estimated to cost the
nation's health care system over $70 billion each year. In New York,
adverse drug events due to errors in written and oral prescriptions
carry an annual cost to the health care system of approximately $130
million.

Part 63.6(a)(7) of the State Education Commissioner's regulations
currently allows prescriptions for non-controlled substances to be
electronically transmitted from a practitioner to a pharmacy, provided
the transmission is secured through electronic encryption.  PHL § 3338
currently authorizes the prescribing and dispensing of controlled
substances pursuant to electronic prescriptions in accordance with DOH
regulations which require that such prescriptions be transmitted in a
transmission format acceptable to DOH. Similarly, PHL§ 3308 authorizes
DOH to promulgate regulations regarding the prescribing, dispensing,
use and transmission of electronic prescriptions. This legislation
makes clarifications to this existing statutory authority to promote
the electronic prescribing and dispensing of controlled substances.

In promoting electronic prescriptions for controlled substances, the
bill preserves certain existing safeguards, such as the provision that
no more than a 30-day supply of a controlled substance may be
dispensed in conjunction with an electronic prescription, unless the
prescription indicates that such period is authorized under DOH
regulations. In addition, the bill requires that any controlled
substance dispensed in accordance with an electronic prescription be
labeled in a specific manner, which mirrors the requirements already
in existence for nonelectronic prescriptions for controlled
substances. This will clarify and conform the existing statutory
authority in PHL §§ 3308 and 3338 for dispensing of electronic
prescriptions for controlled substances,

D. Updating Controlled Substance Schedules

Entries on the State schedules are not the same as those that appear
on the five federal schedules of controlled substances (21 U.S.C. §
801). Chapter 457 of the Laws of 2007 made conforming changes that
brought the Article 33 schedules closer to the federal schedules, but
they still are not identical. Drug-seeking individuals often exploit
the fact that certain drugs classified as controlled substances under
federal law are not controlled substances under New York law and are
more easily diverted. For example, DOH is aware of increasing
diversion and abuse of the pain reliever pregabalin, a federal
Schedule V controlled substance not defined as a controlled substance
by State law. Analysis of prescription information reveals that
numerous individuals who seek controlled substances from multiple
practitioners also seek prescriptions for pregabalin.

In 2006, the United States Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) updated its
definition of anabolic steroids in conjunction with the Anabolic
Steroid Control Act of 2004. This federal law was enacted to prevent
abuse of anabolic steroids by professional athletes and to address
widespread abuse of anabolic steroids and their precursors by college,
high school, and middle school students. The law added 59 additional
steroids and their precursors to the list of anabolic steroids defined
as controlled substances and closed a loophole exploited by anabolic
steroid traffickers, who were marketing steroid precursors (steroid
substances that are converted to anabolic steroids in the body) and
designer steroids (steroid substances containing a minor chemical
modification) as dietary supplements. Such dietary supplements have
the same effect in the body as anabolic steroids and were readily
available in health food stores without a prescription. Bringing the
New York State scheduling and definition of anabolic steroids into
conformity with federal scheduling will curtail illegal sale of these
dangerous drugs marketed as dietary supplements.

A major national investigation of sales of anabolic steroids conducted
by DOH also found that along with steroids, human growth hormone was
particularly prone to abuse. DOH investigators recently seized from a
Brooklyn pharmacy $7.5 million worth of human growth hormone and other
anabolic steroids. Records indicated that the pharmacy dispensed an
estimated $30 million worth of human growth hormone over the past
year. Human growth hormone is not a controlled substance under federal
law at this time, but it is appropriate to add it to the state
schedule to curtail its diversion and abuse.

E. Methadone Treatment Programs
Current law requires MMTPs to submit monthly records of methadone
activity to DOH.  This is unnecessary. The Office of Alcohol and
Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) registers and regulates MMTPs in New
York and requires that they comply with specific recordkeeping
requirements regarding methadone usage. Specifically, OASAS requires
MMTP records to include signed physician orders and to document the
administration, dispensing, and receipt of methadone by authorized
persons. MMTPs must document the amount of methadone they use each day
and must complete a report documenting a daily inventory of narcotics
on hand, The rigorous accountability demanded by OASAS obviates the
need for DOH to receive monthly MMTP records of methadone usage.
However, it will still be necessary for an MMTP to immediately notify
DOH in the event of the loss, theft, or possible diversion of
controlled substances.

 BUDGET IMPLICATIONS :

This bill is not anticipated to have a fiscal impact on the State,
except that electronic prescribing will reduce the number of
prescriptions written on official New York State prescription forms,
which are paid for by the State.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This bill will take effect immediately, except that §§ 1 through 3 and
21 will take effect 180 days after the bill's enactment and §§ 14
through 20 will take effect 10 days after the bill's enactment.

illegal sale of anabolic steroids and pregabalin by designating them

maintains the requirement that the pharmacy electronically file

Section 12 of the bill amends PHL 3381 to authorize electronic

or possible diversion of controlled substances be immediately
reported. The section also removes a reference to Article 23 of the

Section 20 of the bill provides that the bill will take effect
immediately, except that §§ 3 and 19 will take effect 180 days after
the bill's enactment and §§ 13 through 18 will take effect 90 days
after the bill's enactment. Section 20 of the bill also grants
immediate authority to the Department to add, amend, or repeal
regulations necessary for the implementation of the legislation, and
states that any provisions providing for or addressing the provision

specifically permitted by the federal government.
